pr_chain.title: Normalize model names between local and remote manifests for migration diffing
pr_chain.description:
When running `sozo migrate --world 0x...`, the migration system always detects differences between the local and remote manifests even when there are none, causing unnecessary transactions to be sent. The root cause is a naming mismatch: local manifest model names are fully qualified (e.g., `dojo_mock::models::model`, always in snake_case from the Cairo compiler), while remote manifest model names are derived from emitted events which only contain the struct name in PascalCase (e.g., `Model`). This makes the `WorldDiff::compute` comparison always fail to match models, so every model appears as changed.

    The goal of this task is to make the local and remote model names comparable in `WorldDiff::compute` by normalizing the local model's fully-qualified name to the same short PascalCase form used by the remote manifest. This is a temporary fix; the issue of fully-qualified name comparison should be revisited in a future change (see discussion about using array of felts or `ByteArray`).

    Please also update the existing tests to reflect this normalization behavior and add coverage to ensure that comparing a local manifest (with fully-qualified snake_case model names) against a remote manifest (with PascalCase short model names) produces no diff when the class hashes match.

## Environment Setup
This is a Rust workspace (see root `Cargo.toml`). The relevant crate is `crates/dojo-world`. Check the root `Cargo.toml` and `crates/dojo-world/Cargo.toml` for dependency setup. Look at the `Makefile` (if present, otherwise check `CONTRIBUTING.md`) and the CI workflow `.github/workflows/ci.yml` for how the project is built and tested. Also check `rust-toolchain.toml` for the required Rust version and `rustfmt.toml`/`clippy.toml` for formatting/linting configs.

## Implementation Plan
1.  Open `crates/dojo-world/src/migration/world.rs`. In the `WorldDiff::compute` function, locate the closure that matches remote models against local ones (the `.find(|e| e.name == model.name)`).
    2.  Before this match, derive a `model_name` from the local `model.name`:
        - Use `split("::")` and take the last segment to get the short name.
        - Use `convert_case` (already a dependency, see `Cargo.toml`) to convert from `Case::Snake` to `Case::Pascal`. Note: the `convert_case` crate is already listed as a workspace dependency in `crates/dojo-world/Cargo.toml`.
        - Use `unwrap_or(&model.name)` as a fallback if splitting fails (e.g., no `::`).
    3.  Replace the comparison `e.name == model.name` with `e.name == model_name`.
    4.  Make sure the `use convert_case::{Case, Casing};` import is added at the top of `world.rs`.
    5.  Update `crates/dojo-world/src/migration/world_test.rs`:
        - In `no_diff_when_local_and_remote_are_equal`, the local model is named `"dojo_mock::models::model"` (snake_case fully-qualified). The remote manifest should now have a model with name `"Model"` (PascalCase short name) and the same class hash.
        - In `diff_when_local_and_remote_are_different`, remote models should use PascalCase short names (`"Model"` and `"Model2"`) while local models stay fully-qualified snake_case (`"dojo_mock::models::model"`, `"dojo_mock::models::model_2"`).
    6.  Update `crates/dojo-world/src/manifest_test.rs`:
        - In `fetch_remote_manifest`, after loading both local and remote manifests, compute the diff using `WorldDiff::compute` and assert `diff.count_diffs() == 0`.
        - Import `WorldDiff` from `crate::migration::world::WorldDiff`.
        - For the local manifest, load from the path to `manifest.json` in the artifacts directory (already present in the test as `deploy_world` returns the artifacts path).
    7.  Review the `Cargo.toml` change: it only reformats the `cainome` dependency list — verify it doesn't alter functionality. This is likely an incidental formatting change from `rustfmt`; you may keep or revert it, but ensure formatting is consistent.

pr_chain.title: Add ensure_abi method to generated model contracts
pr_chain.description:
The Cairo compiler strips ABI entries for types that are not directly referenced by an entry point's input or output. This means that a Dojo model type is only present in the ABI of its generated contract if at least one system uses it in a function signature. This is a problem: `dojo-bindgen` needs the ABI of **every** model to generate bindings at compile time.

The goal is to guarantee that every model's type (and any inner type it references) appears at least once in the ABI of the model's generated contract. We will do this by adding a new `#[external(v0)]` method named `ensure_abi` to the contract that the `#[derive(Model)]` plugin generates. This method takes the model type itself as an input parameter, which forces the compiler to emit the type's ABI entry.

The method body can be empty — its only purpose is to reference the type so the ABI entry is populated. Note that if a system already uses the model, the type may then appear more than once in the ABI; that is acceptable.

## Expected changes

1. **In `crates/dojo-lang/src/model.rs`**: the `handle_model_struct` function generates the contract code. Add a new external function `ensure_abi` to the generated contract module. Place it after the existing `schema` method. The signature should be:
   - `fn ensure_abi(self: @ContractState, model: $type_name$) {}` where `$type_name$` is the model's Rust type name (the same interpolation variable already used for other generated methods).

2. **Update the golden test data** in `crates/dojo-lang/src/plugin_test_data/model` so the expanded code and diagnostic expectations match the new generated code (the new method adds one more "Unsupported attribute" diagnostic per model, and appears in the expanded code block after `schema`).

3. **Update the manifest test data** in `crates/dojo-lang/src/manifest_test_data/manifest` — the generated ABI for each model contract now includes a `function` entry named `ensure_abi` with an input of the model's type, plus `struct`/`enum` ABI entries for the model type and its inner types. Also update the corresponding `class_hash` values.

4. **Update the version references** in `crates/dojo-lang/src/manifest_test_data/compiler_cairo_v240/Scarb.lock` and `examples/spawn-and-move/Scarb.lock` from `0.4.4` to `0.5.0`.

5. **Update the expected class hash** in `crates/dojo-world/src/contracts/model_test.rs` to match the new generated contract (the class hash changes because the contract code changes).

6. **Update `examples/spawn-and-move/Scarb.lock`** — bump the `dojo_examples` version next to the `dojo` dependency bump (see the diff in the repo).

## Environment Setup
Check the following repo files to understand how to build and test:
    - `Cargo.toml` (root workspace, Rust crates)
    - `crates/dojo-lang/Cargo.toml` and `crates/dojo-world/Cargo.toml` for the crates you'll modify
    - `crates/dojo-lang/README.md` and `crates/dojo-lang/Scarb.toml` for Cairo/Scarb specifics
    - `.github/workflows/ci.yml` and `scripts/` (e.g. `scripts/cargo_test.sh`, `scripts/cairo_test.sh`, `scripts/clippy.sh`) for how tests are typically run
    - `rust-toolchain.toml` for the Rust toolchain

## Implementation Plan
1. Open `crates/dojo-lang/src/model.rs` and locate the `handle_model_struct` function.
    2. In the generated contract module string (inside `RewriteNode::interpolate_patched`), add the following after the existing `schema` external function:
       ```
       #[external(v0)]
       fn ensure_abi(self: @ContractState, model: $type_name$) {
       }
       ```
       Note: `$type_name$` is already an interpolation key used in this template — no new map entries are needed.
    3. Regenerate/update the golden test file `crates/dojo-lang/src/plugin_test_data/model`:
       - The diagnostic section will now show one additional `error: Unsupported attribute.` for the `#[external(v0)]` on `ensure_abi` for each model (Position, Roles, OnlyKeyModel, Player).
       - In the `expanded_cairo_code` section, add the new method block inside each generated contract, right after the `schema` method.
    4. Update `crates/dojo-lang/src/manifest_test_data/manifest`:
       - For each model contract (`moves`, `position`, etc.), add the new `function` ABI entry for `ensure_abi` and the associated `struct`/`enum` ABI entries for the model type and its member types.
       - Update the `class_hash` values for the affected contracts.
    5. Update `crates/dojo-lang/src/manifest_test_data/compiler_cairo_v240/Scarb.lock`: change `dojo` version from `0.4.4` to `0.5.0`.
    6. Update `examples/spawn-and-move/Scarb.lock`: change `dojo_examples` version from `0.4.4` to `0.5.0`.
    7. Update `crates/dojo-world/src/contracts/model_test.rs`: change the expected `position.class_hash()` hex value to the new hash that results from the added method.
    8. Run the relevant test suites to verify the changes.

When waiting for a transaction to be confirmed, we sometimes get a TransactionHashNotFound error even though the transaction status already showed it as accepted. This seems to happen with load-balanced RPC providers where the node handling the status check isn't the same one that processed the transaction yet. We should make the waiter retry on that specific error instead of failing immediately, and probably bump the default timeout since this can add extra delay.

pr_chain.title: Implement entity deletion handling in Torii core processors
pr_chain.description:
We need to implement handling for entity deletion events in the Torii indexer. Currently, the system only processes `StoreSetRecord` events that create or update entities, but when entities are deleted from the world via the `delete!` macro, the indexer does not remove the corresponding records from its SQLite database. This causes stale data to remain in the indexer's storage.

    The goal is to:
    1. Create a new `StoreDelRecordProcessor` that listens for `StoreDelRecord` events emitted by the world contract.
    2. Implement the `delete_entity` method in the SQL layer that removes an entity and all its nested/related records from the database.
    3. Ensure the processor is registered in both the Torii binary and the test setup.

    You'll need to examine the existing `StoreSetRecordProcessor` to understand the pattern for event processing, and the `set_entity` method in `sql.rs` to understand how entities are currently stored. The deletion logic must handle nested structures (structs within structs) similar to how `build_set_entity_queries_recursive` handles them for creation.

## Environment Setup
This is a Rust workspace. Check the following files for build and test configuration:
    - `Cargo.toml` (workspace root) for workspace configuration
    - `crates/torii/core/Cargo.toml` for the torii-core crate dependencies
    - `crates/torii/graphql/Cargo.toml` for the graphql crate dependencies
    - `crates/torii/types-test/Cargo.toml` and `crates/torii/types-test/Scarb.toml` for the test project configuration
    - Review `CONTRIBUTING.md` and `.github/workflows/ci.yml` for build and test instructions

## Implementation Plan
1. **Update `crates/torii/core/src/processors/mod.rs`**:
       - Add `pub mod store_del_record;` to the module declarations
       - Define shared constants `MODEL_INDEX` and `NUM_KEYS_INDEX` (currently defined locally in `store_set_record.rs`)

    2. **Create `crates/torii/core/src/processors/store_del_record.rs`**:
       - Implement `StoreDelRecordProcessor` as a struct deriving `Default`
       - Implement the `EventProcessor` trait with:
         - `event_key()` returning `"StoreDelRecord"`
         - `validate()` checking that the event has exactly one key
         - `process()` that:
           - Parses the model name from `event.data[MODEL_INDEX]`
           - Retrieves the model schema from the database
           - Extracts keys from the event data (starting from `NUM_KEYS_INDEX + 1`)
           - Calls `db.delete_entity(keys, entity_schema)`
           
    3. **Update `crates/torii/core/src/processors/store_set_record.rs`**:
       - Remove the local `MODEL_INDEX` and `NUM_KEYS_INDEX` constants
       - Import these from the parent module instead

    4. **Update `crates/torii/core/src/sql.rs`**:
       - Replace the existing `delete_entity` method signature from `(model: String, key: FieldElement)` to `(keys: Vec<FieldElement>, entity: Ty)`
       - Implement the new `delete_entity` method:
         - Compute the `entity_id` using `poseidon_hash_many` on the keys
         - Build the table path from the entity name
         - Call a new recursive helper `build_delete_entity_queries_recursive`
         - Execute all queued delete queries
       - Create `build_delete_entity_queries_recursive`:
         - For `Ty::Struct`: enqueue a `DELETE FROM [table] WHERE entity_id = ?` query for the current path, then recurse into struct members
         - For `Ty::Enum`: recurse into all enum options
         - For `Ty::Primitive`: do nothing (no child tables)
       - Use `query_queue.push_front` to ensure parent tables are deleted before child tables (foreign key constraints)

    5. **Update `crates/torii/core/src/query_queue.rs`**:
       - Add a `push_front` method that prepends to the queue (mirroring `enqueue` but using `push_front`)

    6. **Update `bin/torii/src/main.rs`**:
       - Import `StoreDelRecordProcessor`
       - Add it to the `event` processors vector

    7. **Update `crates/torii/graphql/src/tests/mod.rs`**:
       - Import `StoreDelRecordProcessor`
       - Add it to the test engine's processors
       - Add a `delete` function to the test records contract that removes a record and its subrecords
       - Execute a delete transaction during test setup

    8. **Update `crates/torii/types-test/src/contracts.cairo`**:
       - Add `fn delete(self: @TContractState, record_id: u32)` to the `IRecords` trait
       - Implement the `delete` function that fetches the record, sibling, and subrecord, then calls the `delete!` macro

    9. **Update `crates/torii/graphql/src/tests/models_test.rs`**:
       - Add a deleted record test verifying that after deletion, the record is no longer returned by GraphQL queries
       - Add helper query functions for `recordSiblingModels` and `subrecordModels`

    10. **Update `crates/torii/types-test/Scarb.lock`** — bump the `types_test` package version (no manual edit needed; this updates automatically when Scarb runs).

pr_chain.title: Refactor torii GraphQL object traits into BasicObject and ResolvableObject
pr_chain.description:
The `ObjectTrait` in the torii GraphQL module is currently used for both resolvable objects (like Transaction, Entity, Event, etc.) and non-resolvable objects (like PageInfo, Connection, Edge, etc.). This causes the trait to have many optional methods that are often unused, and it forces non-resolvable objects to implement dummy `resolve_one`/`resolve_many` methods that always return `None`.

    Your task is to refactor this design by splitting `ObjectTrait` into two separate traits:

    1. `BasicObject` — a trait for all GraphQL objects that defines the shared, non-resolver behavior:
       - `name(&self) -> (&str, &str)` — singular/plural name
       - `type_name(&self) -> &str`
       - `type_mapping(&self) -> &TypeMapping`
       - `related_fields(&self) -> Option<Vec<Field>>` (default `None`)
       - `objects(&self) -> Vec<Object>` — the method that builds the GraphQL object(s) from the type mapping and related fields (move this logic from the current `ObjectTrait` implementation).

    2. `ResolvableObject: BasicObject` — a trait for objects that expose query resolvers:
       - `resolvers(&self) -> Vec<Field>` — returns the resolver fields for the object (single and/or plural queries).
       - `subscriptions(&self) -> Option<Vec<SubscriptionField>>` (default `None`)
       - `input_objects(&self) -> Option<Vec<InputObject>>` (default `None`)
       - `enum_objects(&self) -> Option<Vec<Enum>>` (default `None`)
       - `connection_objects(&self) -> Option<Vec<Object>>` — the method that builds the connection/edge object types if the object has plural resolvers (move logic from the current `connection()` method).

    Additionally, you should reduce code duplication in the resolver implementations by introducing two shared helper functions in `crates/torii/graphql/src/object/mod.rs`:

    - `resolve_one(table_name: &str, id_column: &str, name: &str, type_name: &str, type_mapping: &TypeMapping) -> Field` — a generic single-object resolver that fetches a single row by the given column.
    - `resolve_many(table_name: &str, id_column: &str, name: &str, type_name: &str, type_mapping: &TypeMapping) -> Field` — a generic plural resolver that fetches a page of rows and builds a connection output.

    Then update all existing object implementations to use these new traits and helpers:
    - Non-resolvable objects (EdgeObject, ConnectionObject, PageInfoObject, ContentObject, SocialObject) should implement `BasicObject`.
    - Resolvable objects (EntityObject, EventObject, MetadataObject, ModelObject, ModelDataObject, TransactionObject) should implement `ResolvableObject` and use the new helper functions where applicable.
    - Add a `TRANSACTION_HASH_COLUMN` constant in `constants.rs` (value `"transaction_hash"`) and a `PAGE_INFO_NAMES` constant (value `("pageInfo", "")`) so that hardcoded strings are replaced with named constants.

    Finally, update `schema.rs` to work with the new trait design. Introduce an `ObjectVariant` enum:

    ```rust
    pub enum ObjectVariant {
        Basic(Box<dyn BasicObject>),
        Resolvable(Box<dyn ResolvableObject>),
    }
    ```

    The `build_schema` function should:
    - Return a `Vec<ObjectVariant>` from `build_objects` (boxes of either `BasicObject` or `ResolvableObject`).
    - Iterate over the objects, register their `objects()`, and for `Resolvable` variants also:
      - Add their `resolvers()` to the query root.
      - Register their `connection_objects()`, `enum_objects()`, and `input_objects()`.
      - Add their `subscriptions()` to the subscription root.
    - The `subscription_root` should be built once before the loop and populated inside it.

    Ensure the refactor preserves the existing GraphQL schema behavior (same query fields, types, subscriptions, and connections), with no changes to the public API.

## Environment Setup
Check `crates/torii/graphql/Cargo.toml` for crate-specific dependency details. The root `Cargo.toml` and `crates/torii/Cargo.toml` may list workspace-level dependencies. `rust-toolchain.toml` specifies the Rust toolchain. For general contribution guidelines, see `CONTRIBUTING.md`. Test configuration may be driven by `Cargo.toml`/`crates/torii/graphql/Cargo.toml` (cargo test).

## Implementation Plan
1. In `crates/torii/graphql/src/object/mod.rs`:
       - Rename `ObjectTrait` to `BasicObject` and remove `resolve_one`, `resolve_many`, `table_name`, and `connection` from it.
       - Move the current `objects()` implementation (building the object from type mapping) into `BasicObject` as a provided method.
       - Add the new trait `ResolvableObject: BasicObject` with methods: `resolvers(&self) -> Vec<Field>`, `subscriptions(&self) -> Option<Vec<SubscriptionField>>` (default `None`), `input_objects(&self) -> Option<Vec<InputObject>>` (default `None`), `enum_objects(&self) -> Option<Vec<Enum>>` (default `None`), and `connection_objects(&self) -> Option<Vec<Object>>` (default `None`).
       - Move the `connection()` method logic from the old `ObjectTrait` into `connection_objects()` on `ResolvableObject`, keeping the `EdgeObject`/`ConnectionObject` creation.
       - Add the `ObjectVariant` enum as described.
       - Copy the existing `resolve_one`/`resolve_many` default implementations from `ObjectTrait` into standalone public helper functions `resolve_one(...)` and `resolve_many(...)` that take explicit `table_name`, `id_column`, `name`, `type_name`, and `type_mapping` parameters (as shown in the diff).
    2. In `crates/torii/graphql/src/constants.rs`:
       - Add `pub const TRANSACTION_HASH_COLUMN: &str = "transaction_hash";`
       - Add `pub const PAGE_INFO_NAMES: (&str, &str) = ("pageInfo", "");`
    3. In `crates/torii/graphql/src/object/connection/edge.rs`:
       - Replace `ObjectTrait` with `BasicObject`.
       - Remove the `resolve_one`/`resolve_many` override stubs (rely on the trait defaults).
    4. In `crates/torii/graphql/src/object/connection/mod.rs`:
       - Replace `ObjectTrait` with `BasicObject` in the `impl` for `ConnectionObject`. No other changes needed there.
    5. In `crates/torii/graphql/src/object/connection/page_info.rs`:
       - Replace `ObjectTrait` with `BasicObject`.
       - Replace the hardcoded name `("pageInfo", "")` with `PAGE_INFO_NAMES` and the type name `"World__PageInfo"` with `PAGE_INFO_TYPE_NAME`.
       - Remove the `resolve_one`/`resolve_many` stubs.
    6. In `crates/torii/graphql/src/object/metadata/content.rs` and `crates/torii/graphql/src/object/metadata/social.rs`:
       - Replace `ObjectTrait` with `BasicObject`.
       - Remove the `resolve_one`/`resolve_many` stubs.
    7. In `crates/torii/graphql/src/object/entity.rs`:
       - Implement `BasicObject` (keep `related_fields`).
       - Implement `ResolvableObject` and use the helper functions:
         - `resolve_one` with `ENTITY_TABLE`, `ID_COLUMN`, `self.name().0`, `self.type_name()`, `self.type_mapping()`.
         - `resolve_many` with `ENTITY_TABLE`, `EVENT_ID_COLUMN`, `self.name().1`, `self.type_name()`, `self.type_mapping()`.
       - Add the `keys_argument` to the many-resolver field.
       - Return `vec![resolve_one_field, resolve_many_field]` from `resolvers()`.
    8. In `crates/torii/graphql/src/object/event.rs`:
       - Implement `BasicObject`.
       - Implement `ResolvableObject` and use the `resolve_many` helper with `EVENT_TABLE`, `ID_COLUMN`.
       - Keep `subscriptions()` on the `ResolvableObject` impl.
       - Return `vec![resolve_many_field]` from `resolvers()`.
    9. In `crates/torii/graphql/src/object/model.rs`:
       - Implement `BasicObject` (keep `type_mapping`).
       - Implement `ResolvableObject`, using `resolve_one` (with `MODEL_TABLE`, `ID_COLUMN`) and `resolve_many` (with `MODEL_TABLE`, `ID_COLUMN`).
       - Add the `order` argument to the many-resolver field (as done in the current code).
       - Keep `input_objects()`, `enum_objects()`, and `subscriptions()` on the `ResolvableObject` impl.
    10. In `crates/torii/graphql/src/object/metadata/mod.rs`:
       - Implement `BasicObject`.
       - Implement `ResolvableObject`, keeping the custom plural resolver that uses `row_types()` and `metadata_connection_output`. Replace the internal `table_name` variable with `METADATA_TABLE` directly.
       - Ensure `input_objects`/`enum_objects`/`connection_objects` are not needed here (return defaults).
    11. In `crates/torii/graphql/src/object/model_data.rs`:
       - Implement `BasicObject` and override `objects()` (the recursive data object builder + `entity_field()`).
       - Implement `ResolvableObject` and use the `resolve_many` helper with `EVENT_ID_COLUMN` for the id column. Keep the custom `where`/`order` arguments.
       - Remove the now-redundant `OBJECT` trait methods.
    12. In `crates/torii/graphql/src/object/transaction.rs`:
       - Implement `BasicObject` (nothing special).
       - Implement `ResolvableObject` and use `resolve_one` with `TRANSACTION_TABLE`, `TRANSACTION_HASH_COLUMN`, and `resolve_many` with `TRANSACTION_TABLE`, `ID_COLUMN`.
       - Remove the local `COLUMN` constant (now `TRANSACTION_HASH_COLUMN`).
    13. In `crates/torii/graphql/src/schema.rs`:
       - Change `build_objects` to return `Vec<ObjectVariant>` and wrap each object accordingly:
         - `Box::new(EntityObject)` → `ObjectVariant::Resolvable(Box::new(EntityObject))`
         - `Box::new(EventObject)`, `ModelObject`, `MetadataObject`, `TransactionObject`, `ModelDataObject` → `Resolvable`
         - `Box::new(SocialObject)`, `ContentObject`, `PageInfoObject` → `Basic`
       - Refactor `build_schema` to register objects, populate `query_root` from `resolvers()`, register connection/enum/input objects, and populate `subscription_root` — all within a single loop over `ObjectVariant`.

pr_chain.title: Extend Torii indexer to support L1 handler transactions and add transaction type column
pr_chain.description:
The Torii indexer currently only processes `Invoke` transactions. This limits the indexer's ability to capture events and transaction data from other transaction types, such as `L1Handler` transactions, which are common in cross-chain messaging scenarios. Additionally, the `transactions` table does not distinguish between different transaction types, making it difficult to query or filter based on the type.

    Your task is to:
    1. Update the transaction processing pipeline in `crates/torii/core/src/engine.rs` to handle `Transaction::L1Handler` in addition to the existing `Transaction::Invoke` handling.
    2. Refactor the processor traits and implementations in `crates/torii/core/src/processors/` to accept a generic `TransactionReceipt` and `Transaction` instead of type-specific `InvokeTransactionReceipt` and `InvokeTransactionV1`.
    3. Update `Sql::store_transaction` in `crates/torii/core/src/sql.rs` to support both `Invoke` and `L1Handler` transaction types, and to store the transaction type in the `transactions` table.
    4. Add a SQL migration to add a `transaction_type` column to the `transactions` table with a default value of `'INVOKE'` for backwards compatibility.
    5. Improve the resilience of block processing — if a block fails to process, log the error and retry rather than crashing the sync loop.

## Environment Setup
This is a Rust workspace. Check the root `Cargo.toml` for workspace configuration. The Torii indexer code is in `crates/torii/core/` — see `crates/torii/core/Cargo.toml` for its dependencies. SQL migrations are in `crates/torii/migrations/`. For testing, look at `crates/torii/core/src/sql_test.rs` and existing tests. Setup and CI workflows are described in the root `.github/workflows/ci.yml` and `CONTRIBUTING.md`. Use `cargo test` after building — the repository uses `rust-toolchain.toml` to pin the toolchain version.

## Implementation Plan
- Review `crates/torii/core/src/engine.rs` — modify the `process` method to extract the transaction hash from both `Invoke` (specifically `V1`) and `L1Handler` transaction variants, then call a unified transaction/receipt processing method.
    - Refactor the `EventProcessor` and `TransactionProcessor` traits in `crates/torii/core/src/processors/mod.rs` to use `&TransactionReceipt` and `&Transaction` instead of `&InvokeTransactionReceipt` and `&InvokeTransactionV1`. Update all implementations in `metadata_update.rs`, `register_model.rs`, `store_del_record.rs`, `store_set_record.rs`, and `store_transaction.rs` accordingly.
    - Update `Sql::store_transaction` in `crates/torii/core/src/sql.rs` to accept a `&Transaction` and extract appropriate fields for both `Invoke` and `L1Handler` variants. Add the transaction type as a new column in the INSERT statement.
    - Create a new migration file `crates/torii/migrations/YYYYMMDDHHMMSS_add_txn_type.sql` that adds a `transaction_type` TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'INVOKE' column to the `transactions` table.
    - Wrap the block processing call in `sync_range` with a match statement — on error, log the error and continue (retry on next sync iteration) instead of propagating the error up.

The current configuration references job name patterns that do not match the actual job names defined in the repository's CI workflows (e.g., `.github/workflows/check.yaml` and `.github/workflows/test.yaml`). This causes Mergify to fail to detect successful CI runs and blocks automatic merging of approved pull requests.

pr_chain.title: Improve missing dependency reporting and end-to-end test coverage
pr_chain.description:
Enhance the error reporting when a build environment cannot be created due to a missing dependency, and add an end-to-end test that verifies this behavior.

    Currently, when `wheels.BuildEnvironment()` fails to install the combined build system and build backend dependencies, the error is raised as a generic `subprocess.CalledProcessError` without detailed information about which dependency is missing. This makes it difficult for users to diagnose the root cause.

    Implement the following changes:
    1. In `src/fromager/sdist.py`, modify the `prepare_build_environment` function to catch `subprocess.CalledProcessError` when creating the `BuildEnvironment`. Parse the pip error output to identify the missing dependency name (look for the pattern "Could not find a version that satisfies the requirement <name>"). If a match is found, raise a `MissingDependency` exception with the appropriate details. If no match is found, re-raise the original exception.
    2. Rework `e2e/test_report_missing_dependency.sh` to be self-contained and runnable via tox. The test should:
       - Bootstrap a known package (stevedore 5.2.0) to generate a build order file
       - Extract build dependencies from the build order
       - Remove build dependencies from the local wheel repository
       - Rebuild the wheel mirror with the remaining packages
       - Build the original package and verify it fails with a `MissingDependency` error
       - Verify the error output is logged correctly
    3. Update `.github/workflows/test.yaml` to include the new `report_missing_dependency` test script in the e2e test matrix.
    4. Update `.mergify.yml` to require the new e2e test jobs (`e2e (3.11, report_missing_dependency)` and `e2e (3.12, report_missing_dependency)`) to pass before automatic merge.

## Environment Setup
Check `pyproject.toml` for package metadata and dependencies, `tox.ini` for test environments and commands, and `.github/workflows/test.yaml` for CI test configuration. Review existing e2e test scripts in the `e2e/` directory (e.g., `e2e/test_bootstrap.sh`, `e2e/common.sh`) to understand test conventions and helpers.

## Implementation Plan
1. Modify `src/fromager/sdist.py` to add a regex pattern for parsing pip's missing dependency messages.
    2. Wrap the `wheels.BuildEnvironment` instantiation in a try/except block that catches `subprocess.CalledProcessError`, parses the output, and raises `MissingDependency` when appropriate.
    3. Rewrite `e2e/test_report_missing_dependency.sh` to be self-contained, using tox for all operations (bootstrap, source download, wheel build) and jq for parsing build order JSON.
    4. Update `.github/workflows/test.yaml` to add `report_missing_dependency` to the test-script matrix.
    5. Update `.mergify.yml` to include the new e2e test jobs in the automatic merge conditions.

pr_chain.title: Pin tox environments to Python 3.11 to prevent accidental old interpreter use
pr_chain.description:
Some of our tox environments — specifically `linter`, `cli`, and `pkglint` — currently rely on whatever Python interpreter tox happens to discover, which can vary depending on the system PATH. This can lead to environments being created with an older Python version than intended, potentially causing subtle issues like linters running under a different interpreter than CI, CLI commands testing against an unexpected runtime, or packaging checks validating against the wrong Python version.

    The goal is to explicitly pin these specialized environments to `python3.11` so they consistently use that interpreter regardless of what else is on the PATH. The default `py` environment should remain unset so it continues to pick up `python3` from the PATH, which allows developers to easily run tests against a newer Python version when desired (e.g. 3.12 or 3.13).

    Please ensure the change is limited to the tox configuration and does not alter any source code or test logic. The repository should continue to support Python 3.11 as the primary development target, while remaining flexible for manual testing against newer versions via the default environment.

## Environment Setup
Review `tox.ini` for the tox environment definitions. Check `pyproject.toml` for project metadata and dependency declarations (including test/dev extra requirements). The `Makefile` (if present) or GitHub workflow files (`.github/workflows/check.yaml`, `.github/workflows/test.yaml`) may provide additional context on how CI invokes tox and tests, but the core changes should be confined to `tox.ini`.

## Implementation Plan
- Open `tox.ini` and locate the `[testenv:linter]`, `[testenv:cli]`, and `[testenv:pkglint]` sections.
    - Add a `base_python = python3.11` line to each of these three environment definitions, placing it alongside existing settings like `deps` and `commands`.
    - Leave the `[testenv]` base section and the default `py` environment unchanged — no `base_python` set there so it continues to resolve `python3` from the PATH.
    - Verify the `[tox]` header's `envlist` still lists `py,linter` and that the `e2e` environment (which inherits from `[testenv]`) is unaffected.
    - After editing, run the tox environments locally to confirm they activate with Python 3.11 and all existing checks (lint, CLI smoke test, packaging validation) pass.

pr_chain.title: Change E2E test wheel server port to avoid system conflicts
pr_chain.description:
The end-to-end test scripts currently use port 9090 for the local wheel server that simulates a PyPI mirror. This port collides with the Cockpit web console service on RHEL and Fedora systems, causing the E2E tests to fail when they try to bind to the port. Cockpit is a common default service on these operating systems, making the current port choice unreliable for CI environments and developer machines running these distributions.

    Please update both E2E test scripts to use a different port that is less likely to conflict with common system services. The goal is to make the E2E test suite more portable and reliable across different Linux distributions and CI setups.

## Environment Setup
Review the `pyproject.toml` and `tox.ini` files in the repository root for project configuration, dependency management, and test environment setup instructions. The E2E scripts themselves (`e2e/test_build_with_build_order.sh` and `e2e/test_report_missing_dependency.sh`) contain the current port usage and can be run after setting up the tox environment as described in the project documentation.

## Implementation Plan
1. Identify the current port usage (9090) in both `e2e/test_build_with_build_order.sh` and `e2e/test_report_missing_dependency.sh`.
    2. Select a new port that is unlikely to conflict with common system services (e.g., 9999 or another port outside the well-known service range).
    3. Update all occurrences of the port number in the `python3 -m http.server` command and the `WHEEL_SERVER_URL` environment variable in both test scripts.
    4. Ensure the new port is consistently used in all references within each script and across both scripts.
    5. Run the E2E tests to verify they pass with the new port configuration.

pr_chain.title: Extend fromager support and CI to Python 3.10
pr_chain.description:
The goal is to broaden fromager's compatibility so that it can be used with Python 3.10, which is required for Intel Gaudi's SynapseAI/HabanaLabs 1.15 toolchain.

    Please ensure that the project explicitly declares Python 3.10 support in its project metadata and that the CI pipeline tests both unit and end-to-end functionality on that version. Specifically, this involves updating:
    
    1. The project's `requires-python` constraint and PyPI classifiers
    2. The test fixture package's `requires-python` constraint and PyPI classifiers
    3. The GitHub Actions test matrix to include Python 3.10
    4. The Mergify merge rules to require the new Python 3.10 CI checks
    
    This change should be minimal and focused — no other behavior or features should change.

## Environment Setup
The repository uses `pyproject.toml` for project metadata and dependency declarations, and `tox.ini` for test environment configuration. The GitHub Actions workflow `.github/workflows/test.yaml` also contains CI setup details. Consult these files to understand installation and test procedures.

## Implementation Plan
1. Edit the root `pyproject.toml`:
       - Change `requires-python = ">=3.11"` to `requires-python = ">=3.10"`.
       - Add `"Programming Language :: Python :: 3.10"` to the `classifiers` list.
    2. Edit the test fixture `e2e/flit_core_override/pyproject.toml`:
       - Change `requires-python = ">=3.11"` to `requires-python = ">=3.10"`.
       - Add `"Programming Language :: Python :: 3.10"` to the `classifiers` list.
    3. Edit `.github/workflows/test.yaml`:
       - Add `"3.10"` to the `python-version` matrix for both the `unit` and `e2e` jobs.
    4. Edit `.mergify.yml`:
       - Add the new required check names for the Python 3.10 unit and e2e tests to the automatic merge conditions.

pr_chain.title: Write constraints.txt file alongside build-order.json output
pr_chain.description:
Modify the WorkContext class in `src/fromager/context.py` to also write a `constraints.txt` file in the work directory, alongside the existing `build-order.json` file. The constraints file should contain one line per build step in the format `dist==version` (e.g., `stevedore==5.2.0`), matching the `dist` and `version` fields stored in the build order. This file should be written whenever the build order is updated, and it should be consumable by pip as a constraints file.

## Environment Setup
Check `pyproject.toml` for project dependencies and packaging configuration. Check `tox.ini` for test environment configuration and how the test suite is organized. The end-to-end test script is at `e2e/test_bootstrap.sh`.

## Implementation Plan
1. In `src/fromager/context.py`, locate the `__init__` method of the `WorkContext` class.
    2. Add a new instance attribute `self._constraints_filename = self.work_dir / 'constraints.txt'` right after the existing `self._build_order_filename` line.
    3. In the `add_to_build_order` method, after writing the `build-order.json` file (the existing `json.dump` call), add code to open `self._constraints_filename` for writing.
    4. Iterate over `self._build_stack` and write one line per entry using the format `{step['dist']}=={step['version']}\n`.
    5. Ensure the file is overwritten each time (use `'w'` mode, not append mode).

pr_chain.description:

    Please remove the `python-gitlab` entry from the `dependencies` array in `pyproject.toml`. This is a straightforward cleanup that will reduce the project's dependency footprint and avoid unnecessary installations for users.

Review the `docs/develop.md` file for any additional development workflow guidance.

    3. Search the entire source code (`src/` directory) and test files for any imports or references to `gitlab` or `python_gitlab` to confirm nothing else depends on this package.
    4. Verify the change is syntactically valid by running any relevant validation or build checks.
    5. Run the existing test suite to ensure nothing breaks as a result of the dependency removal.

pr_chain.title: Vendor Rust crates into source distributions for offline wheel builds
pr_chain.description:
We need to support building wheels for Python packages that contain Rust code (e.g., `pydantic-core`, `cryptography`, `maturin`, `setuptools-rust`) in environments without network access during the build. Currently, Cargo downloads crates from crates.io at build time, which fails when network access is restricted or unavailable.

    The goal is to vendor all Rust crates into the source distribution (sdist) during the source preparation step, and configure the build to use those vendored crates with `CARGO_NET_OFFLINE=true`. This ensures wheel builds are reproducible and can run offline.

    We need:
    1. A new module that vendors Rust crates into an sdist directory by running `cargo vendor` and generating the appropriate `.cargo/config.toml`.
    2. The vendored crates must be sanitized to remove pre-compiled archives (`.a` and `.lib` files) to keep the bundle smaller.
    3. The wheel build step must set `CARGO_NET_OFFLINE=true` so Cargo is forced to use the vendored crates.
    4. The `tomli` dependency must be replaced with `toml` because we need TOML write support to generate the Cargo config.
    5. An end-to-end test project using PyO3 must be added so the vendoring workflow is exercised in CI.

    Please check `src/fromager/vendor_rust.py` (new file) for the vendoring logic, `src/fromager/wheels.py` for the build environment change, and `src/fromager/dependencies.py` for the TOML library swap.

## Environment Setup
Check `pyproject.toml` at the repository root for project dependencies and build configuration. Check `tox.ini` at the repository root for test environment configuration. Check `.github/workflows/test.yaml` to understand the CI matrix and how tests run. For the end-to-end test, look at `e2e/pyo3_test/` (a new directory with its own `pyproject.toml` and `tox.ini`).

## Implementation Plan
1. Create a new module `src/fromager/vendor_rust.py` that:
       - Accepts a project directory path.
       - Scans for `Cargo.toml` files.
       - Runs `cargo vendor` with the project directory as the output location (default to a `vendor/` subdirectory).
       - Removes pre-compiled `.a` and `.lib` files from vendored crates and updates their `.cargo-checksum.json` files (make the `shrink_vendored` behavior the default).
       - Generates (or extends) a `.cargo/config.toml` in the project directory pointing `crates-io` to the vendored sources directory.
       - Returns `True` if vendoring was performed (Cargo manifests found), `False` otherwise.
       - Logs progress at info level for visibility.
    2. Update `src/fromager/dependencies.py` to import `toml` instead of `tomli` for `pyproject.toml` parsing.
    3. Update the `build_wheel` function in `src/fromager/wheels.py` to unconditionally set `CARGO_NET_OFFLINE=true` in the extra environment passed to the build backend.
    4. Add a new e2e test fixture under `e2e/pyo3_test/` that is a minimal Python package using PyO3 (a `pyo3_test` extension module).
       - It must include a `Cargo.toml`, `Cargo.lock`, a Rust source file (`rust/lib.rs`), Python package code (`python/pyo3_test/__init__.py`), a `pyproject.toml` using `setuptools-rust`, a `MANIFEST.in` to include Rust sources in sdists, and a `tests.py` for pytest.
       - It must have its own `tox.ini` to run pytest against the built module.
    5. Update `.gitignore` to exclude build artifacts from the e2e PyO3 test fixture (e.g., `.cargo`, `build`, `dist`, `target`, `vendor`).
    6. Update `.github/workflows/test.yaml` to:
       - Add a `rust-version` matrix dimension (e.g., `1.75`, matching RHEL 9.4) and set up the Rust toolchain in both the `unit` and `e2e` jobs.
       - Add a step in the `unit` job to run the PyO3 test's tox environment.

We need to improve error handling and debugging around plugin loading in the overrides module. Make it so we fail loudly with a clear error if a plugin is found but can't be imported, rather than silently ignoring it. Also improve the debug message when no plugin module is found for a package to list the available override modules, and add an info-level log when an override method is successfully found so it's obvious which code path is being taken.

We need to support setting the build variant via the FROMAGER_VARIANT environment variable, in addition to the existing --variant command line option. This makes it easier to specify the variant when running fromager inside containers without having to pass command line arguments. Please make sure the environment variable is used as the default when --variant isn't explicitly provided.

pr_chain.title: Add build log file output for pip wheel builds
pr_chain.description:
Modify the default wheel build process to instruct pip to write a log file containing the output of the build command. The log file should be written to the parent directory of the source distribution root, ensuring the log is preserved when the source tree is cleaned up during bootstrap and making it easy to collect logs across a sequence of builds.

    The log file should be named `build.log` and created in `sdist_root_dir.parent` (the directory containing the source distribution). This will result in paths like `work-dir/<dist>-<version>/build.log` for each package built.

    Update the end-to-end test scripts to verify that these `build.log` files are created for each package during both bootstrap and build-order-driven workflows.

## Environment Setup
Check `pyproject.toml` for project metadata and dependency declarations. Review `tox.ini` for test environment configuration and available test commands/scripts. The e2e test scripts in `e2e/` can also provide insight into how end-to-end tests are structured and executed.

## Implementation Plan
1. Modify `src/fromager/wheels.py` in the `default_build_wheel` function to add a `--log` argument to the pip command list, pointing to `sdist_root_dir.parent / 'build.log'`.
    2. Update `e2e/test_bootstrap.sh` to add the expected `build.log` files to the `EXPECTED_FILES` list for each package (flit_core, pbr, setuptools, stevedore, wheel), using the pattern `work-dir/<dist>-<version>/build.log`.
    3. Update `e2e/test_build_with_build_order.sh` similarly, adding the same expected `build.log` entries to its `EXPECTED_FILES` list.
    4. Ensure the log directory exists or is created as needed (pip should create the file, but verify the parent directory exists — in the context of fromager, `sdist_root_dir.parent` should already exist as the work-dir package directory).

pr_chain.title: Switch build environment creation to virtualenv and activate it for subprocesses
pr_chain.description:
The goal is to make the build environment more reliable and consistent across different Python versions, particularly for tools like maturin that may inspect environment details when performing builds.

Currently, the build environment is created using Python's built-in `venv` module. This has been observed to produce different environment configurations than the `virtualenv` package (especially for Python 3.11), which can cause build tools to incorrectly reference system Python instead of the build environment's Python.

Two changes are needed:

1. **Use `virtualenv` instead of `venv`**: Replace the usage of the standard library `venv.EnvBuilder` with the third-party `virtualenv` package when creating build environments. This requires adding `virtualenv` as a project dependency.

2. **Activate the virtual environment for subprocesses**: When running pip to build a wheel, the subprocess environment needs to be explicitly configured so that tools like maturin:
   - Find the build environment's executables first (via PATH manipulation)
   - Recognize the active virtual environment (via the VIRTUAL_ENV environment variable)

This ensures that any build tools invoked during the wheel build process use the build environment's Python and dependencies rather than falling back to system-wide installations.

## Environment Setup
Check `pyproject.toml` for project dependencies and build configuration. Refer to `tox.ini` and `.github/workflows/test.yaml` for how tests are structured and run.

## Implementation Plan
1. **Add virtualenv dependency**: In `pyproject.toml`, add `"virtualenv"` to the `dependencies` list in the `[project]` section.

    2. **Update imports in `src/fromager/wheels.py`**:
       - Remove `import venv` (no longer needed)
       - Add `import os` and `import sys` (needed for the new logic)

    3. **Modify `BuildEnvironment._createenv` method**:
       - Replace the `venv.EnvBuilder(clear=True, with_pip=True)` creation logic with:
         ```python
         external_commands.run([sys.executable, '-m', 'virtualenv', self.path])
         ```
       - Remove the `self._builder` attribute since it's no longer needed
       - Note that `virtualenv` creates environments with pip by default and handles clearing existing directories

    4. **Modify `default_build_wheel` function**:
       - Before the `with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory()` block, construct an updated environment:
         - Get the existing PATH from `extra_environ` or `os.environ`
         - Prepend the build environment's bin directory (`build_env.python.parent`) to PATH
         - Set the `VIRTUAL_ENV` environment variable to the build environment path
       - Create a new `override_env` dictionary that starts as a copy of `extra_environ` and includes the updated PATH and VIRTUAL_ENV values
       - Pass `override_env` instead of `extra_environ` to `external_commands.run()`

pr_chain.title: Restructure CLI commands into click groups and separate modules
pr_chain.description:
The current CLI relies on `argparse` with all command handlers defined in `src/fromager/__main__.py` as a monolith. This makes it harder to add new high-level commands later. Restructure the command-line interface so that:

    1. The CLI framework switches from `argparse` to `click` (add `click` as a dependency).
    2. The step-by-step commands (`download-source-archive`, `prepare-source`, `prepare-build`, and `build`) are grouped under a new `step` command group, so they are invoked as `fromager step download-source-archive ...`, etc.
    3. The `build` command is renamed to `build-wheel` within that `step` group.
    4. Each top-level command (`bootstrap`, `step`, `canonicalize`, `build-order`) is moved into its own module under a new `src/fromager/commands/` package.
    5. The `fromager` console script entry point is updated to point to a new `invoke_main` function (which is a thin wrapper around the click group).
    6. Global options (verbose, log-file, sdists-repo, wheels-repo, work-dir, patches-dir, envs-dir, settings-file, wheel-server-url, cleanup) are handled at the top-level click group and passed down to subcommands via context object.
    7. The `bootstrap` command gets a `--variant` option directly on it (moved from the top-level global options).
    8. The `build-order` subcommands (`as-csv`, `summary`, `graph`) are grouped under a `build-order` click group.
    9. Exception logging behavior is preserved — wrap the clicked command invocation so that exceptions are logged with `logger.exception()` before propagating.

    Also update:
    - `README.md` to document the new command syntax (`step download-source-archive`, `step prepare-source`, `step prepare-build`, `step build-wheel`).
    - End-to-end test scripts `e2e/test_build_with_build_order.sh` and `e2e/test_report_missing_dependency.sh` to use the new command names.
    - Test files: replace `tests/test_main.py` with `tests/test_bootstrap.py` that tests the helper function for parsing requirements arguments (factored out into the new bootstrap module).

## Environment Setup
Check `pyproject.toml` for the project's declared dependencies (add `click` to the `dependencies` list). For test/development setup, review `tox.ini` to understand test environments and commands. Look at `tests/conftest.py` for pytest fixtures. For e2e tests, refer to the shell scripts under `e2e/` and how they invoke `tox`.

## Implementation Plan
- Add `click` to `dependencies` in `pyproject.toml`.
    - Create `src/fromager/commands/__init__.py` and new module files: `bootstrap.py`, `step.py`, `canonicalize.py`, `build_order.py`.
    - Move command handler logic from `src/fromager/__main__.py` into the new modules, converting decorators to click commands/groups.
    - Refactor `src/fromager/__main__.py` to define a click group with global options, create the `WorkContext` and pass it as `obj` to subcommands via `@click.pass_obj`, and add an `invoke_main()` entry point.
    - Extract requirements parsing logic from tests into a helper in `bootstrap.py` and update tests accordingly (rename `tests/test_main.py` to `tests/test_bootstrap.py`).
    - Update README and e2e shell scripts to reflect the new CLI syntax (`step` prefix and `build-wheel` rename).

pr_chain.title: Update auto-merge rules for expanded CI test matrix
pr_chain.description: The CI test matrix has been expanded to include Python 3.10 and a Rust version dimension, which changed the names of the check jobs. The automatic merge rules in the repository configuration need to be updated to reference the new job names and to ensure that the Python 3.10 jobs are required for merging. This will keep the auto-merge functionality working correctly with the updated test suite.

pr_chain.title: Fix tarfile extractall filter argument compatibility issue
pr_chain.description:
We need to make the `unpack_source()` function in `src/fromager/sources.py` compatible with all supported Python versions. Currently, the code calls `t.extractall(unpack_dir, filter='data')` on tar files, but the `filter` parameter for `TarFile.extractall()` was only added in Python 3.12. On older Python versions (3.8-3.11), this call will fail with a `TypeError` because the method doesn't accept this keyword argument.

The goal is to check whether the `extractall()` method actually supports the `filter` parameter before passing it. When supported, we should continue using `filter='data'` (which provides security benefits against path traversal attacks). When not supported (older Python versions), we should call `extractall()` without the filter parameter and log a debug message indicating so.

Please look at the function signature of `extractall()` using `inspect.signature()` to determine at runtime whether the `filter` parameter is accepted. This approach avoids hardcoding Python version checks and works across any environment.

## Environment Setup
Check the `pyproject.toml` file at the repository root for project metadata and dependency information. The `tox.ini` file contains test environment configuration. The `Makefile` (if present) may have common development commands, but the primary build and test configuration is in `pyproject.toml` and `tox.ini`.

## Implementation Plan
1. Add `import inspect` to the imports at the top of `src/fromager/sources.py`.
    2. Create a helper function `_takes_arg(f, arg_name)` that uses `inspect.signature()` to check if a function accepts a given parameter name.
    3. In `unpack_source()`, modify the `.tar.gz` branch to:
       - First check if `t.extractall` accepts a `filter` parameter using the helper function.
       - If it does, call `t.extractall(unpack_dir, filter='data')` as before.
       - If it doesn't, log a debug message explaining that it's unpacking without the filter, then call `t.extractall(unpack_dir)` without the filter argument.
    4. Ensure the existing behavior remains unchanged on Python 3.12+ where the filter parameter is supported.

pr_chain.title: Eliminate redundant candidate name checks in package finders
pr_chain.description: Many package names produce identical values after canonicalization or other name transformations, causing the finder functions to check the same candidate repeatedly. Convert the candidate name lists in the sdist, wheel, and source directory finders to sets so duplicate values are automatically removed before the search loop runs. This avoids wasted filesystem checks and keeps the search logic clean without altering its behavior.

instruction:
## Migrate Jenkins CI infrastructure from Windows Server 2019 to 2022

We need to fully migrate our Jenkins CI testing infrastructure from Windows Server 2019 (WS2019) to Windows Server 2022 (WS2022). Windows Server 2019 is being phased out, and we need to ensure all our testing pipelines, infrastructure builds, and Docker image creation are running on the newer, supported platform.

    The goal is to update all Jenkins pipeline files and configuration to:
    1. Use WS2022 agent labels for all Windows-based testing stages
    2. Remove any references to WS2019-specific Azure images, Docker images, or agent labels
    3. Update the Windows Docker base image from `ltsc2019` to `ltsc2022`
    4. Ensure the Azure managed images build process only creates WS2022 images
    5. Update all test stage names and function calls to reference WS2022 instead of WS2019

    This migration should be completed across the entire `.jenkins` directory structure, ensuring consistency between the main Jenkinsfile, infrastructure pipelines, and test-specific pipeline definitions.

## Environment Setup
Review the Jenkins pipeline configuration files in the `.jenkins` directory structure. Key files to examine include:
    - `.jenkins/Jenkinsfile` - Main Jenkins pipeline entry point
    - `.jenkins/infrastructure/` - Infrastructure build and Docker image pipelines
    - `.jenkins/library/vars/` - Shared Groovy variables and test functions
    - `.jenkins/pipelines/` - Platform-specific and test-specific pipelines

    These are Jenkins declarative pipelines (Groovy), so there are no traditional dependency installation steps. The repository uses standard GitHub checkout procedures for Jenkins builds.

## Implementation Plan
1. **Update `globalvars.groovy`**: Remove all WS2019 agent label entries and update the WS2022 labels. This is the central registry for agent labels used across all pipelines.
    2. **Update main `Jenkinsfile`**: Replace all parameter references from `WS2019_NONSGX_CUSTOM_LABEL` to `WS2022_NONSGX_CUSTOM_LABEL` and remove `WS2019_DCAP_CFL_LABEL`/`WS2019_DCAP_ICX_LABEL` parameters that are no longer needed.
    3. **Update infrastructure pipelines** (`build_azure_managed_images.Jenkinsfile`, `build_docker_images.Jenkinsfile`, `build_windows_docker_images.Jenkinsfile`, `publish_docker_images.Jenkinsfile`):
       - Remove WS19 entries from `AZURE_IMAGES_MAP` and `OS_NAME_MAP`
       - Update default agent labels from `ws2019-nonsgx` to `ws2022-nonsgx`
       - Update Docker image references from `oetools-ws2019` to `oetools-ws2022`
       - Update stage names and documentation comments
    4. **Update Windows Dockerfile**: Change base image from `mcr.microsoft.com/windows/servercore:ltsc2019` to `mcr.microsoft.com/windows/servercore:ltsc2022`
    5. **Update `tests.groovy`**: Change all `ws2019-nonsgx` agent label references to `ws2022-nonsgx` in Windows nonSGX test stages
    6. **Update `e2e_testing.Jenkinsfile`**: Remove WS2019 parameter definitions and their references when triggering downstream builds
    7. **Update Azure Windows pipeline** (`.jenkins/pipelines/Azure/Windows/Jenkinsfile`): Change all test stage names from Win2019 to Win2022, update agent labels to use `acc-win2022-dcap` and `acc-v3-win2022-dcap`, and ensure the `windowsLinuxElfBuild` function call has the correct parameters
    8. **Update test pipelines** (`.jenkins/pipelines/OpenEnclave/intel/tests/windows.Jenkinsfile` and `.jenkins/pipelines/OpenEnclave/releases/tests/Jenkinsfile`): Change agent labels from `acc-win2019-dcap` to `acc-win2022-dcap` and update stage names from "Windows Server 2019" to "Windows Server 2022"

pr_chain.title: Update Azure DCAP Client to 1.12.3 and fix CI image creation issues
pr_chain.description:
We need to update the Azure DCAP client dependency from version 1.12.2 to 1.12.3 across both Linux and Windows build environments. Additionally, the CI infrastructure for creating Azure managed images has several issues that need to be addressed:

    1. **Azure DCAP client version bump**: The DCAP client package (Microsoft.Azure.DCAP) needs to be updated from 1.12.2 to 1.12.3 in all installation scripts and Ansible roles. This applies to both the Linux Ubuntu package and the Windows NuGet package.

    2. **Packer plugin installation**: The Linux managed image build process fails because the required Packer plugins (for Azure and Ansible) are not installed. The Jenkins pipeline needs to install these plugins after installing Packer itself.

    3. **Windows VM provisioning flags**: The Windows managed image build creates VMs with conflicting flags. The `--security-type Standard` flag is currently passed but the VM size `Standard_DC4s_v2` may not be optimal, and the flag ordering causes issues. The pipeline should use `Standard_DC2s_v2` size and ensure `--security-type Standard` is properly specified.

    4. **Windows Update blocking issue**: During Windows image creation on Azure VMs, Windows Update (KB5034439) fails because Azure VMs don't use WinRE (Windows Recovery Environment). This causes the image creation to fail. The Ansible playbook should exclude this specific update when running on Azure VMs.

    5. **Ansible variable for Azure VMs**: The Windows Ansible role needs a variable `is_azure_vm` that controls whether certain Windows updates are excluded. This should be set when provisioning on Azure VMs (from Jenkins) but default to false for other environments.

    6. **Windows Update handling refactor**: The Windows Updates task in the Ansible role needs to be refactored to use a handler for rebooting instead of inline reboot logic, and to conditionally apply the exclude list.

## Environment Setup
The developer should examine the following repo files to understand the build and test setup:
    - `scripts/ansible/requirements.txt` - Ansible dependencies
    - `CMakeLists.txt` - Main build configuration
    - Any `Makefile`, `tox.ini`, or CI configuration files in the root directory
    - The `tests/` directory structure for understanding test organization
    - `.jenkins/infrastructure/` for CI pipeline configuration

## Implementation Plan
1. **Update Azure DCAP client version**:
       - Edit `scripts/ansible/roles/linux/az-dcap-client/vars/ubuntu/main.yml` to change `az_dcap_client_version` from `"1.12.2"` to `"1.12.3"`
       - Edit `scripts/ansible/roles/windows/openenclave/vars/main.yml` to update `az_dcap_client_url` and `az_dcap_client_hash` to the 1.12.3 versions
       - Edit `scripts/install-windows-prereqs.ps1` to update the `AzureDCAPNupkgURL` and `AzureDCAPNupkgHash` parameters to 1.12.3

    2. **Fix Packer plugin installation in Jenkins pipeline**:
       - Edit `.jenkins/infrastructure/build_azure_managed_images.Jenkinsfile` in the `buildLinuxManagedImage` function
       - In the `Check Prerequisites` stage, after installing Packer, add commands to install the `github.com/hashicorp/azure` and `github.com/hashicorp/ansible` plugins

    3. **Fix Windows VM provisioning flags**:
       - Edit `.jenkins/infrastructure/build_azure_managed_images.Jenkinsfile` in the `buildWindowsManagedImage` function
       - Change the VM size from `Standard_DC4s_v2` to `Standard_DC2s_v2`
       - Reorder the `--security-type Standard` flag to be passed after `--nsg-rule NONE`
       - Add a comment noting that trusted launch security types are not supported for managed image capture

    4. **Add Azure-specific Windows update exclusion**:
       - Edit `scripts/ansible/roles/windows/openenclave/vars/main.yml` to add a new variable `azure_windows_update_reject_list` containing `[ "KB5034439" ]` with a comment explaining Azure VMs don't use WinRE

    5. **Refactor Windows Updates handling in Ansible role**:
       - Edit `scripts/ansible/roles/windows/openenclave/tasks/main.yml` to:
         - Remove the inline reboot logic and `always` block

pr_chain.title: Upgrade Ansible to version 8 and adjust Python dependency handling
pr_chain.description:
Update the Ansible-based infrastructure provisioning tooling to use Ansible 8.x (with ansible-core 2.15.x) and its compatible dependencies. This involves:

    1. Bumping the `ansible`, `ansible-core`, `cryptography`, `pyOpenSSL`, and `pywinrm` versions in `scripts/ansible/requirements.txt`.
    2. Updating the `install-ansible.sh` script to:
       - Support only apt-get (remove yum support).
       - Require Python 3.9-3.11 (Ansible 8 compatibility).
       - Auto-detect or install a supported Python version.
       - Use `sudo` for privileged apt-get commands only, so the script can run as a regular user.
       - Explicitly use `python3` and `python-is-python3` packages (removing the generic `python` package dependency).
    3. Updating `remove-ansible.sh` to:
       - Remove Ansible collections from `~/.ansible/collections/`.
       - Detect the Python version used by the installed Ansible and uninstall the Python packages accordingly.
       - Remove yum support.
    4. Updating `ansible.cfg` to use user-local temp directories (`~/.ansible/tmp`) instead of `/tmp/.ansible`.
    5. Removing the `clang-10` and `clang-format-10` packages from the Ubuntu focal package list in `scripts/ansible/roles/linux/openenclave/vars/ubuntu/focal.yml`, while adding `python3` and `python-is-python3`.
    6. Pinning the `azure-cli` package to version `2.56.0-1~focal` in the Jenkins Azure image build pipeline to avoid breaking changes from version 2.57.0.
    7. Fixing the Windows agent labels in `.jenkins/library/vars/globalvars.groovy` to use the correct Azure VM labels (`SGXFLC-Windows-2022-DCAP-v2` and `SGXFLC-Windows-2022-DCAP-v3`).

## Environment Setup
- Check `scripts/ansible/requirements.txt` for the Python package dependencies.
    - Look at `scripts/ansible/install-ansible.sh` and `scripts/ansible/remove-ansible.sh` for how Ansible is installed/removed on the system.
    - The `.jenkins/infrastructure/build_azure_managed_images.Jenkinsfile` and `.jenkins/library/vars/globalvars.groovy` define CI pipeline behavior.
    - The `scripts/ansible/roles/linux/openenclave/vars/ubuntu/focal.yml` file lists Ubuntu package dependencies for the Ansible role.
    - Since this is a CI/infrastructure change, there is no standard C/C++ build system or unit test suite to run. Tests are validation scripts and manual verification of the bash scripts.

## Implementation Plan
1. Edit `scripts/ansible/requirements.txt`:
       - Update `cryptography` from `41.0.6` to `42.0.5`.
       - Update `pyOpenSSL` from `23.2.0` to `24.0.0`.
       - Change `ansible>=4.10,<=5.2.0` to `ansible>=8.7,<9.0`.
       - Add `ansible-core>=2.15.5,<2.16`.
       - Change `pywinrm>=0.3.0` to `pywinrm==0.4.3`.

    2. Rewrite `scripts/ansible/install-ansible.sh`:
       - Remove the yum branch and its error message.
       - Detect the current Python 3 version and check if it's one of `3.9`, `3.10`, or `3.11`.
       - If not supported, use `apt-cache` to find and install a supported version via `wait-apt-get install libssl-dev libffi-dev python3-pip python<version> -y`.
       - If no supported version can be found or installed, print an error and exit.
       - Use `sudo apt-get` for apt commands (inside `wait-apt-get`).
       - Use `${PYTHON_EXECUTABLE} -m pip` instead of `pip3` for upgrading pip and installing requirements.

    3. Rewrite `scripts/ansible/remove-ansible.sh`:
       - Remove the yum branch and its error message.
       - Check for installed Ansible collections in `~/.ansible/collections/ansible_collections/` (community.general, ansible.windows, community.windows) and remove them with `rm -rf`.
       - Use `ansible --version` to detect the Python version, then use `python<version> -m pip uninstall -r "$DIR/requirements.txt" -y`.
       - If Ansible is not found, print a message and skip uninstallation.

    4. Edit `scripts/ansible/ansible.cfg`:
       - Change `remote_tmp` and `local_tmp` from `/tmp/.ansible` to `~/.ansible/tmp`.

    5. Edit `scripts/ansible/roles/linux/openenclave/vars/ubuntu/focal.yml`:
       - Remove `python`, `clang-10`, and `clang-format-10` from `apt_distribution_packages`.
       - Add `python3` and `python-is-python3`.

    6. Edit `.jenkins/infrastructure/build_azure_managed_images.Jenkinsfile`:
       - In the "Install Azure CLI" stage, after `sudo apt-get update`, add a line to show available azure-cli versions (`apt-cache show azure-cli | grep Version`).
       - Change the install line to `sudo apt-get -y install azure-cli=2.56.0-1~focal jq`.

    7. Edit `.jenkins/library/vars/globalvars.groovy`:
       - Change the default label for `acc-win2022-dcap` from `"SGXFLC-Windows-2022-DCAP"` to `"SGXFLC-Windows-2022-DCAP-v2"`.
       - Change the default label for `acc-v3-win2022-dcap` from `"ACC-v3-SGXFLC-Windows-2022-DCAP"` to `"SGXFLC-Windows-2022-DCAP-v3"`.

pr_chain.title: Fix leap year date generation in attestation validity tests
pr_chain.description:
The test suite for attestation report and evidence verification generates dates that are offset by ±1 year from the current time or from validity boundaries. When the original date is February 29th (leap day), shifting the year by ±1 produces an invalid date (e.g., February 29, 2014), which causes `oe_datetime_is_valid` to fail and tests to break. This only manifests on leap days (e.g., February 29, 2024).

    The goal is to make all date-offset operations in the test code produce valid dates, regardless of whether the current date or validity boundary is February 29th. When a year is added or subtracted and the resulting date would be February 29th in a non-leap year, the day should be adjusted (e.g., set to February 28th) to keep the date valid. Additionally, the `oe_datetime_log` function in `common/datetime.c` should be made robust so that logging failures to convert a datetime to a string do not crash or produce undefined behavior—instead, they should log an error message.

    Specifically:
    - In `tests/attestation_plugin/plugin/tests.c`, both `_test_time` and `_test_time_policy` decrement `year` by 1 on the `from` date and increment `year` by 1 on the `until` date. Add guards so that if the resulting date is February 29th, the day is set to 28.
    - In `tests/report/common/tests.cpp`, the `past` and `future` datetimes are constructed from the current time with a ±10 year offset, and the `valid_from`/`valid_until` dates are shifted by ±1 year. For the `past`/`future` datetimes, use an arbitrary fixed day (e.g., day 10) instead of the current day of month to avoid the leap year issue. For the `valid_from`/`valid_until` shifts, add guards so that February 29th becomes February 28th.
    - In `common/datetime.c`, update `oe_datetime_log` to check the return value of `oe_datetime_to_string`. If it fails, log an error message with the result string; otherwise, log the converted string as before.

    No production logic changes are needed—only test date generation and logging robustness.

## Environment Setup
Check the repository's build and test configuration files:
    - `CMakeLists.txt` at the repo root for top-level build configuration.
    - `tests/CMakeLists.txt`, `tests/attestation_plugin/CMakeLists.txt`, and `tests/report/CMakeLists.txt` (if present) for how the affected tests are built and registered.
    - Look for any `Makefile`, `tox.ini`, `pyproject.toml`, or `setup.py` in the root listing to see if alternative build/test commands are available. Follow the instructions in those files to install dependencies and run the test suite.

## Implementation Plan
- Open `common/datetime.c` and modify `oe_datetime_log` to capture the return value of `oe_datetime_to_string`. On success, log the verbose message as before; on failure, log an error with the result code.
    - Open `tests/attestation_plugin/plugin/tests.c` and locate `_test_time` and `_test_time_policy`. After decrementing `tmp.year` or `dt.year` (for `from`) and after incrementing `tmp.year` or `dt.year` (for `until`), add a check: if `month == 2 && day == 29`, set `day = 28`.
    - Open `tests/report/common/tests.cpp` and locate the `past` and `future` `oe_datetime_t` initializations. Replace `(uint32_t)timeinfo.tm_mday` with a fixed value like `10` in both initializers, with a comment explaining why.
    - In the same file, after `valid_from.year -= 1` and after `valid_until.year += 1`, add the same leap-day guard: if `month == 2 && day == 29`, set `day = 28`.
    - Build the project and run the affected tests (`tests/attestation_plugin` and `tests/report`) to confirm they pass, especially with the system date set to a leap day or by simulating it in test logic if feasible.

pr_chain.title: Install trace.h and log.h headers for oehostverify component

## Implementation Plan

    2. Keep the existing ungated `install()` statements for these headers as-is to maintain current behavior for the main component.

pr_chain.title: Update comment for malloc visibility and add aligned_alloc test
pr_chain.description:
We need to improve the documentation and test coverage for the Open Enclave libc implementation. Specifically:

    1. The comment in `libc/CMakeLists.txt` explaining why `malloc.c` is exposed with default visibility is currently vague ("for aligned_alloc and free"). It should be clarified to explain that these symbols are pulled in as part of the `openenclave/corelibc/bits/malloc.h` inclusion, which is more accurate and helps future maintainers understand the dependency chain.

    2. The `tests/module_loading/module/module.c` test file verifies that various libc symbols are visible/exported from the enclave. Currently it checks for `posix_memalign` but not `aligned_alloc`. Since `aligned_alloc` is also part of the malloc family that gets exported, we should add a check for it to ensure the symbol remains visible. Note: while `posix_memalign` could potentially be removed (the symbol is still visible), we should keep it for now and just add the new check to avoid breaking anything.

    This is a minor improvement but ensures the codebase is well-documented and tested for the symbols we intentionally export.

## Environment Setup

    - `CMakeLists.txt` (top-level) for overall build configuration
    - `libc/CMakeLists.txt` for the specific libc build rules
    - `tests/CMakeLists.txt` for test registration
    - `tests/module_loading/CMakeLists.txt` for the module_loading test specifics

## Implementation Plan
1. In `libc/CMakeLists.txt`, locate the `DEFAULT_VISIBILITY` list (around line 974) and update the comment next to `malloc.c` to read: `# for aligned_alloc and free that are pulled in as part of openenclave/corelibc/bits/malloc.h inclusion`
    2. In `tests/module_loading/module/module.c`, find the `test_libc_symbols()` function
    3. Add `TEST_SYMBOL(aligned_alloc);` after the existing `TEST_SYMBOL(posix_memalign);` line
    4. Verify the change is consistent with the existing style (alphabetical-ish ordering of the checks — `aligned_alloc` should come before `free`)

instruction:
## Handle OpenBSD lack of SetKeepAlivePeriod support in keepalive listener

We need to make the keepalive listener code work correctly on OpenBSD. Currently, the `keepAliveConn.SetKeepAlivePeriod` method directly calls `TCPConn.SetKeepAlivePeriod`, which is not supported on OpenBSD (see https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/issues/15811). This causes etcd to fail when trying to establish keepalive connections on this platform.

    The goal is to gracefully handle this platform limitation by ignoring `SetKeepAlivePeriod` errors on OpenBSD, while preserving the existing behavior on all other supported platforms. The solution should be clean and maintainable, using Go build constraints to separate platform-specific implementations.

## Environment Setup
Check the repository's `Makefile` for build targets and test commands. The project uses Go modules — review `go.mod` and the `go.mod` files in subdirectories (particularly `client/pkg/go.mod`) for dependency management. Look at `scripts/test.sh` and `scripts/test_lib.sh` for testing conventions.

## Implementation Plan
1. Remove the existing `SetKeepAlivePeriod` method from `keepalive_listener.go` to avoid duplication.
    2. Create a new file `keepalive_listener_unix.go` with build constraint `//go:build !openbsd` that contains the original `SetKeepAlivePeriod` implementation (delegating to `TCPConn.SetKeepAlivePeriod`).
    3. Create a new file `keepalive_listener_openbsd.go` with build constraint `//go:build openbsd` that contains a no-op `SetKeepAlivePeriod` implementation (returning `nil`).
    4. Ensure both new files have the correct copyright header, package declaration, and import of `time` package.
    5. Verify that the `Accept` method in `keepaliveListener` continues to work correctly — on OpenBSD, the `SetKeepAlivePeriod` call will now succeed silently without changing socket options.

pr_chain.title: Add etcdutl hashkv command to compute MVCC key history hash from database snapshot
pr_chain.description:
We need to add a new `hashkv` subcommand to the `etcdutl` command-line tool that allows operators to compute the key-value history hash of an etcd database snapshot file without requiring a running cluster. The goal is to provide a way to verify the integrity of snapshot data and compare it against live cluster state, which is currently only possible via the `etcdctl endpoint hashkv` command against a running member.

    The new command should:
    - Accept a single argument: the path to the etcd database file (e.g., `default.etcd/member/snap/db`).
    - Accept an optional `--rev` flag to specify the maximum revision to hash; a value of 0 should mean the latest revision.
    - Output the computed hash, hash revision, and compact revision in the existing `simple`, `json`, `table`, and `fields` output formats supported by `etcdutl`.
    - Compute the hash using the existing `HashByRev` functionality from the mvcc storage package, which is already exported as part of the `HashStorage` interface.

    Additionally, since the `etcdutl` code lives in a separate module that imports the server storage package, we need to export a constructor for the hash storage implementation currently used internally by the mvcc store so it can be reused outside the server module.

## Environment Setup
- Check `etcdutl/go.mod` and `server/go.mod` for module dependencies and Go version requirements.
    - Refer to the top-level `Makefile` and `scripts/test.sh` / `scripts/test_lib.sh` for how the repository's build and test workflows are orchestrated.

## Implementation Plan
1. In `server/storage/mvcc/hash.go`, export a constructor for the internal hash storage type:
